items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1973-08-06
items.q: you're referring to something like in Jimmy Luster's band, where Si Oliver was the main arranger.

ctx.x: There wasn't any main arrangers. Harold Holmes wrote his. Billy Douglas wrote his. And Herbert Hall. If a guy would get an idea, he would write it down. But no one was, you're referring to something like in Jimmy Luster's band, where Si Oliver was the main arranger.
Well, no, there might be five main arrangers and maybe one guy would only do two.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-09-18
items.q: Well, the reason for that is most all of Jim Lunsford's men were college men.

ctx.x: Well, yeah. Well, the thing I'm getting at, you know, like Lunsford men, they were all gentlemen except Johnny Young said he came up the hard way. Right. And, he was very self-conscious when he went in with the band.
Well, the reason for that is most all of Jim Lunsford's men were college men. Yeah. Or had had some time in college.
Yeah. Well, what about your fellows? How many of them were in college? Do you know?

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1969-12-30
items.q: And Duke Ellington and Cab and Jimmie Lunsford and Andy Craig and all of us were together.

ctx.x: But what about those band leaders when they came then, the musicians? Did they have trouble finding a place to stay? Well, sure they did.

They wouldn't let them go. Well, it was the same way, let me put it this way. The history of the Negro band, such as mine, on the road, is so tragic that sometimes you hate to even recall those days. Because you want to try to forget the things that were done to you. And you would come to town, the first place you would have to look for is the railroad track. Because you knew on the other side of the railroad track is where Negroes lived. And you would be welcomed into their homes over there. But the life of a…
Well, I don't want to pressure you about that business in Thomasville or anything. We can talk about something else if you want to. Well, that's left to you.
